user_prompt:
What is the effect of bupropion, compared with placebo or no bupropion, on smoking cessation at the longest follow-up of at least six months in adults who smoke and are hospitalised (for any reason, including cardiovascular admissions)?

Effect measure: pool as a risk ratio (RR) of being abstinent from smoking, bupropion divided by control, using a random-effects model. RR > 1 means more people quit smoking with bupropion (favours bupropion).

Outcome: the number of participants abstinent from smoking (events) out of the number randomised to each arm (total), at the longest follow-up of six months or more.
- Use the longest follow-up reported that is at least six months (for example 6 or 12 months). Do not use 3-month or earlier results.
- Use the strictest abstinence definition each trial reports: prefer sustained or continuous abstinence, biochemically validated where available; otherwise use point-prevalence abstinence, and state which definition was used. Do not use self-reported "reduced smoking".
- Count everyone randomised in the denominator and treat participants lost to follow-up as still smoking (the standard intention-to-treat rule for smoking trials). If a paper gives the quit rate as a percentage, convert it to a count with the number randomised to that arm.
- If a paper reports only the number analysed in a table, use the randomised numbers from the participant-flow diagram when available, and say which numbers you used.
- Control: placebo or no bupropion (usual care). Exclude trials whose control group receives another smoking-cessation drug (nicotine replacement or varenicline).
- Multi-arm trials: include the bupropion arm and the control arm only; if bupropion is combined with counselling in both arms, compare the arms that differ only by bupropion.
- Assign arms by treatment, not by column position.
- Include only randomised controlled trials in hospitalised adult smokers. Exclude trials in outpatients and trials of non-drug interventions.

Do not pool short-term quitting, adverse events, cardiovascular events, withdrawal symptoms or any other outcome.
